# On Maps, and What They Leave Out

Every map is a decision about what not to say.

This is the first thing that fascinates me about them. A map that included everything would be the world itself, and about as useful. Borges wrote a tiny story about an empire whose cartographers produced a map at a scale of one mile to the mile. It was perfectly accurate and perfectly useless, and later generations abandoned it to rot in the desert. The joke is old, but it holds a real insight: a map works because it lies. It flattens, omits, and simplifies, and it commits to a point of view.

Take the London Underground map, which most people know even if they've never been to London. Harry Beck designed it in 1931 as an electrical engineer, not a cartographer, and his great insight was to ignore geography. The stations sit at tidy intervals, the lines run in straight verticals, horizontals, and forty-five-degree angles, and the Thames becomes a gentle blue ribbon. In reality the distances between stations vary wildly. Some stops that look far apart are a few minutes' walk from each other, and people have famously ridden the train between two stations when walking would have been faster. Beck's map is wrong about space and right about what a traveler underground needs to know: where the lines go, and where they meet. Underground, you don't experience distance. You experience sequence and connection. Beck understood that, and his lie became a more truthful thing than accuracy would have been.

Every map has this quality. It is an argument about what matters.

Consider the Mercator projection, which inflated Greenland to the size of Africa, though Africa is about fourteen times larger. Mercator wasn't being careless. He was solving a real problem for sailors, since his projection preserves angles, so a straight line on the chart corresponds to a constant compass bearing. For navigating a ship in 1569 it was brilliant. But then the map escaped its purpose. It hung on classroom walls for centuries, and generations of children absorbed, without anyone intending it, a picture of the world in which Europe and North America loomed large and the equatorial regions seemed slight. A tool built for one job quietly became a worldview.

I find this a useful warning about all kinds of knowledge. The trouble with a good simplification is that it works so well we forget it's a simplification. We start to mistake the map for the territory, as the phrase goes, and then we're surprised when the territory refuses to behave like the map.

The blank spaces are what really get me, though. Old maps have a particular charm in how they handle ignorance. Medieval mapmakers supposedly wrote *here be dragons* on the edges of the known world, though the phrase is almost certainly a myth, appearing on one globe, the Lenox Globe, as *hic sunt dracones*. What they actually did was more interesting. Sometimes they drew sea monsters, sometimes elephants, sometimes an elaborate ornamental cartouche in the place where knowledge ran out. Some of this was decoration, some was hope, and some was a way of covering embarrassment. A blank spot on a map looks like a failure, and humans have always disliked looking at their own failures.

Modern maps have almost no blank spots, and I wonder whether we've lost something. A satellite image of the Amazon shows every bend of every river. But the image is a surface. It cannot tell you what the forest sounds like at dusk, or which plants the local people use for fever, or where the ground turns to swamp under the canopy. The satellite fills the blank with pixels, and the pixels can trick us into thinking we know the place. Knowing that a location exists is different from knowing it.

There is also the matter of who draws the map. Whoever holds the pen decides what gets a name. When European colonial administrators mapped territories in Africa and Asia, they often ignored existing names, existing boundaries, and existing ways of understanding land. Many communities had no concept of land as a bounded, ownable parcel; their maps, when they made them at all, were often stories, songs, or sequences of landmarks. Aboriginal Australian songlines encode routes across hundreds of miles as verses, so that a traveler who knows the song knows the way, including where to find water. It is a map you carry in your voice rather than on paper. Western cartography had no category for it and was slow to recognize it as navigation at all.

I like this because it broadens the question. What is a map, really? At bottom it's a compressed form of knowledge that lets someone who hasn't been somewhere find their way there. Seen that way, recipes are maps, and so are family stories about how to survive a hard winter. A good teacher's advice is a map of a terrain she has already crossed. Even a proverb is a tiny map with almost all the detail removed and only the warning about the cliff left in.

And like all maps, these can fail. Advice given by someone who crossed the terrain in a different season, or in a different century, may lead you confidently into a swamp. The most useful maps come with a sense of their own limits: a date, a scale, a note about who made them and why. I'd like the same from people. I trust an expert more when she says "this is what I know, and here is where it stops," and I trust a source less when it presents a smooth, unbroken surface of certainty. Honest cartographers have always known to mark the boundary of the surveyed region. Somewhere past it, the coastline is drawn with a dotted line.

That dotted line might be my favorite thing in all of cartography. It says: *someone thinks the shore is here, but no one has confirmed it.* It's a small typographic act of humility. It lets a map be useful and honest at once, giving you something to steer by without pretending the guess is a fact.

If I could ask one thing of everything I read, hear, or believe, it would be to include the dotted lines. Show me where the survey was done and where it was inferred. Let me see the edge of what you know, and I'll trust the interior of your map far more.

Meanwhile the world keeps being larger and stranger than any picture of it, which seems right to me. I'd be a little disappointed if we ever finished the map.
